newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 24.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- WILLIAM COOK CHIEF LAUNCHES SHOCK 80 MILLION POUND BUY-OUT

Andrew Cook, head of steel group William Cook Plc, has launched an 80 million stg buy-out of the firm, which faces a 72 million stg hostile offer from rival Triplex Lloyd. The buy-out vehicle, Steel Casings Investments, is offering 425p cash per share, compared with 386.5p from Triplex Lloyd.
-- ACCOUNTANTS' LIABILITY PLAN UNDER FIRE

Proposals by the big six accountancy firms to set identical limits on their liability in corporate investigations are being opposed by the British Venture Capital Association and the British Bankers' Association. The venture capitalists have sent the agreement between the firms to the restrictive practices court. The bankers are also to complain, and merchant banks are also expected to protest, especially if the accountants attempt to extend the agreement to mergers and acquisitions.
-- PROBE CALL OVER HMSO

Labour public affairs spokesman Derek Foster has called for the National Audit Office to investigate fees paid in the privatisation of Her Majesty's Stationery Office. The call came after a legal battle over 500,000 pounds MA Media Partners says is owed by Electra Fleming, the successful eventual buyers.
THE TIMES
-- INVESTOR BEATS SOCIETY IN COURT OVER UNCOMPETITIVE RATE

Robert Anthony, a small investor with the Norwich and Peterborough Building Society, has won an unprecedented victory in court against the society. Mr Anthony claimed that despite literature promising his account would pay a very competitive rate of interest, he was paid an interestrate near the bottom of recognised league tables. The Norwich County Court judge awarded him 285 pounds stg, a sum equal to the extra interest he would have earned with an average interest rate over the four-year period. The case could lead to millions of investors taking their bank or building society to court over low rates.
-- SEGA SEEKS RETURN OF SONIC BOOM WITH 3 BILLION POUNDS MERGER

Computer games maker Sega has said it will merge with toy maker Bandai in a 3.1 billion-pound stg deal aimed to fight the challenge of Nintendo and Sony. Sega has said it wants to be a global entertainment company and expand further internationally.
Analysts in Japan have seen little merit in the merger.
-- BANK REINFORCES WARNING TO LENDERS ON STANDARDS

The Bank of England has reinforced its warning to high street banks not to lower their lending standards. At a London conference, Michael Foot, the bank's executive director for supervision said banks may not be able to detect the onset of the next downturn and so should not store up bad debt and house repossession problems by making rash lending decisions.
THE GUARDIAN
-- DIAMOND JOBS UNDER THREAT

A thousand jobs in London's Hatton Garden diamond quarter are threated after South African moves employment back home. Gemstone group De Beers, which mines about half the world's diamonds, is expected to come under pressure to relocate its Central Selling Organisation from London to South Africa. The move threatens the British precious stones industry in general.
-- MERSEY MILITANCY THREATENS FORD AND DOCKS

The Transport and General Workers' Union said Ford faces the prospect of serious industrial action over planned job cuts at Halewood, Liverpool. Union officials approved a nationwide strike ballot over Ford's plans to cut a third of the Halewood jobs and transfer all Escort production to the Continent by 2000. Meanwhile, sacked Mersey dockers celebrated international industrial action in protest of the firing of 329 Mersey dock workers 16 months ago after refusing to cross a picket line.
-- SIB BOSS STANDS DOWN AFTER FIVE HARD YEARS

Sir Andrew Large has said he is stepping down after five years as chairman of the Securities and Investments Board. His replacement is likely to be chosen by a Bank of England/Treasury panel. Names in the running include Imro head Phillip Thorpe and Personal Investment Authority chief Colette Bowe. Whoever wins will have to cope with a government more committed to financial regulation, although the SIB's role in this remains unclear.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SHARES ADDS 11 BILLION POUNDS, POUND TAKES A BEATING

The pound fell on foreign exchanges Thursday and shares in London gained 11 billion pounds stg in value. The sterling index against other currencies ended 1.4 points lower at 95.8. Against the mark, the pound was down nearly 5 pfennigs at DM2.6685, and was off more thab two cents against the dollar at $1.6278. The FTSE 100 index gained 52 points to 4,271.5, pushed by a buoyant morning on Wall Street as the financial markets stuck to their assessment that interest rates will not have to increase until after the general election.
-- BRITISH GAS OUTGROWS ITS 150 MILLION POUNDS COMPUTER SYSTEM

Senior industry sources say British Gas's new 150 million-pound customer billing system could soon be unable to cope with the company's planned expansion into the domestic electricity market. The company, which has spent a further 80 million pounds stg to sort out serious glitches in the system, now faces the embarrassing task of developing another computer system to deal with its move into the selling of electricity when the power market opens up to competition in 1998.
-- PEPSICO TO SPIN OFF PIZZA HUT AND KFC

In a bid to compete with Coca-Cola for dominance in the soft drink market, PepsiCo is poised to announce a multi-billion dollar demerger of its Kentucky Fried Chicken, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut restaurants. The demerger prospect was welcomed by shareholders who have long called for PepsiCo to divest its underperforming restaurants.
